headline: OKF brings structured, portable memory for Claude Code agents and teams
summary: OKF (Open Knowledge Format) provides a vendor-neutral way to store project knowledge as markdown files with YAML frontmatter, versioned with code. This allows coding agents and human teams to access consistent, curated information, preventing context loss in n
details: Coding agents often lose context between sessions, forcing them to re-discover project knowledge. This scattered information, from wikis to code comments, doesn't travel with the code or survive new context windows.

Existing solutions like CLAUDE.md or auto-memory have limitations, being either too broad, implicit, or human-centric. There's a clear need for curated, structured team knowledge that's versioned with code and readable by both agents and people.

Open Knowledge Format (OKF) addresses this gap as an open, vendor-neutral format. Announced by Google Cloud in June 2026 (Apache-2.0), it represents knowledge as a directory of markdown files with YAML frontmatter, making it simple and portable.

OKF concepts link via plain markdown, forming a graph of typed, cross-referenced knowledge. This structure is diffable, reviewable in PRs, and portable across tools because it's just text, requiring only YAML frontmatter with a non-empty type.

The okf-skills toolchain, driven by the v0.1 spec, teaches Claude Code agents to use OKF. It ships as a Claude Code plugin and agent skills, installable on Cursor, Codex, and other agents via skills.sh.

Standalone validator and visualizer scripts are also available, working with uv and PyYAML. The visualizer generates a single viz.html with a graph of concepts, a wiki-style detail panel, and deep-linking capabilities.

To enable automatic upkeep, users can paste templates/CLAUDE-okf.md into their project's CLAUDE.md for an opt-in soft mode. This ensures agents consult .okf/ before tasks and write knowledge back after changes.

The core benefit is providing a durable, diffable, and portable home for project knowledge, versioned alongside the code. This prevents agents from repeatedly "forgetting" context, while also creating valuable documentation for human teams.

headline_marked: [[AI-written tests can pass 100% of the time]] but still miss critical bugs, inflating coverage
headline: AI-written tests can pass 100% of the time but still miss critical bugs, inflating coverage
summary: AI-generated tests often pass without verifying actual behavior, creating a false sense of security with high code coverage. This can lead to critical bugs shipping unnoticed.
details: AI-generated tests can pass 100% of the time, yet fail to verify actual code behavior. This creates a 'phantom test' problem, where tests run, turn green, but check nothing useful, leading to bugs shipping unnoticed.

The trap lies in code coverage metrics: a line executed by a useless test counts as much as one genuinely verified. A 90% coverage report can hide a suite of tests that will never fail, even if the code is broken.

LLMs are rewarded for passing tests, not for catching bugs. Without an external oracle, they drift towards soft assertions or cases that never exercise risky branches, taking the shortest path to green.

The countermeasure is simple: before trusting a test, ensure it knows how to fail. Mutate the line it's meant to protect, rerun, and expect it to go red. If it stays green, it's vacant and should be discarded.

Mutation testing automates this process by applying small mutations to code and rerunning the test suite. Any mutation that doesn't make a test fail reveals a 'surviving mutant' – a hole in your test coverage.

This provides a 'mutation score,' indicating the percentage of mutants killed. While coverage tells you if a line is crossed, the mutation score reveals if it's actually tested. The latter is the more critical metric.

A simple rule for AI-generated tests is to never let them enter the suite without proving they can fail. This small cost offers a huge payoff, as a vacant test is worse than no test at all, lulling developers into false security.
